https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-dozens-kil.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J2V7 Among the biggest factors fueling the conflict is the scarcity of land and resources shared by herders and farmers Image: Ute Grabowsky/photothek.de/picture alliance Advertisement Local officials say at least 25 people were murdered on Monday night by armed men who stormed the village of Bin-Per, in the Mangu local government area of Nigeria 's Plateau state. Perpetrators reportedly moved from house to house, killing residents with machetes. Women and children accounted for most of the victims. Resident Muftwan Yamput told France's AFP news agency that he and his family "survived by a whisker." "But," he added, "my neighbors were attacked. Two people killed in their house." Cycle of reprisals in Nigeria attacks Monday night's massacre followed the killing of two herders last week. Those were in turn followed by a suspected reprisal targeting the nearby village of Maitimbe, where multiple houses were torched. The Mwaghavul Youth Movement, a local ⁠advocacy group, ​has accused authorities of ​failing to protect vulnerable communities. "The ‌recurring destruction of communities, killing of innocent citizens, burning of homes and destruction of farmlands cannot continue ​to be treated ⁠as ordinary incidents," said the group's spokesperson on Sunday while calling for a review of security ​in the area. Matthew Kwarpo, a representative in the Plateau state assembly, called on authorities to, "deploy proactive measures in preventing or mitigating unnecessary attacks before they occur," especially in Mangu. "The incident underscores the urgent need for concerted efforts to address the underlying grievances and prevent further escalation of violence in the affected communities," said Kwarpo. The Fulani land dispute: Impact in northern Nigeria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Amnesty says President Tinubu not fulfilling promise to 'enhance security' The incidents of the last week are the continuation of years of spiraling violence between nomadic Muslim ethnic Fulani herders and mainly Christian farmers over access to increasingly scarce land and resources in central Nigeria's Middle Belt region. Land grabbing over mineral and mining resources, political and economic tensions between locals and outsiders, and the influx of hardline Muslim and Christian preachers have all fueled divisions . Plateau has also seen hundreds killed in urban riots between religious groups in recent years. In May 2025, rights group Amnesty International (AI) estimated that at least 2,630 people had been killed in Plateau state alone in the two years since President Bola Tinubu had taken office on the promise of enhancing security. The group said authorities had instead failed "to protect the rights to life, physical integrity, liberty and the security of tens of thousands of people across the country." Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP View image in fullscreen A NSW parliamentary committee found in July that DPP Sally Dowling had given false evidence on a media leak about a young offender. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP New South Wales politics NSW top prosecutor Sally Dowling and state attorney general discussed which barristers could review her office, estimates hears Dowling tells budget estimates that Michael Daley called to tell her he was appointing a senior counsel and ‘raised quite a number of names’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Tue 1 Sep 2026 03.47 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 23.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The top prosecutor in New South Wales says she discussed a list of barristers to lead an independent review into controversial findings against her office with the state’s attorney general, before he appointed someone she had known “professionally and socially” for nearly 30 years. Last month, a state parliamentary committee voted 4-3 to find that the NSW director of public prosecutions (DPP), Sally Dowling SC, had given false evidence about the pitching of a story about an Indigenous child performing an acknowledgment of country at a sentencing hearing to radio station 2GB. Dowling admitted her office had pitched the story, but denied she had authorised it. The NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, and the DPP rejected the committee’s findings. NSW’s top prosecutor gave false evidence on media leak about young Indigenous offender, inquiry finds Read more At budget estimates on Monday, Dowling said that she and Daley had spoken before Noel Hutley SC was appointed to lead an independent review, which found there was “no positive basis” to find she had given false evidence. She said Daley had “called me to tell me that he was appointing a senior counsel to review the evidence that was before the inquiry and its report of the majority”. “He raised quite a number of [senior counsel’s] names that he was considering, including Mr Hutley’s name, and some of those people did have a conflict, they had acted for the ODPP (Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions), for me, and that was about the extent of the discussion.” Dowling said Daley had not asked for “advice”. “He mentioned some names, and I responded to those names,” she said. Dowling said of the list of eight to 12 people, she said two “would not be appropriate”, but did not raise Hutley as inappropriate as she did not believe there was a conflict of interest. Under further questioning, Dowling said she had indicated to Daley that she knew Hutley, but had not given any further detail. Dowling, who told estimates she first met Hutley when she came to the bar in 1997, said she knew “most of the senior members of the inner bar after 30 years in Sydney”. Asked if she and Hutley were friends, she said: “I know him professionally and socially and have utter respect for his professionalism, and if Mr Hutley considered that he had some kind of conflict that meant that he shouldn’t accept that from the attorney general, I have total confidence that he would have informed the attorney general of that.” Dowling said her signing a statement of support for Hutley’s candidacy for the NSW bar council in 2015 did not give rise to a conflict, saying she was one of 26 other barristers who signed the letter “10 years ago”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion She said none of the names she discussed with Daley were interstate lawyers. Asked if it would have been more appropriate for someone from interstate to write the review, she said: “It’s a matter for the attorney general whom he seeks advice from.” On Monday morning, Daley told estimates he rejected the suggestion that Dowling and Hutley were friends. He said he had “full and absolute confidence” in Dowling and that Hutley’s review, in which Hutley was assisted by two other barristers, had provided “an objective and expert analysis of [the report’s] shortcomings”. Asked if it was appropriate for him to consult with Dowling about barristers to conduct the review, a spokesperson for Daley said “the attorney general holds regular discussions with the Director of Public Prosecutions about relevant matters”. Hutley was contacted for comment.
